> I'm not in support of such a subjective rubric for success. I believe metrics are an effective tool here, and that quantified expectations of return are also helpful. 
If this is the key point of contention then we do have an impasse. This is not idle opinion either, I have actual experience of why this will not do what you hope it will and will backfire in ways you cannot predict. 

The issue you have, is **metrics are subjective**. 

One example: my previous company had a £2m grant from Google as part of a much larger funding project called YouTube Originals that set metrics at the start.

Our grant, and a subsequent grant, was tied to a few metrics:

- Number of minutes produced 
- We had a target 
- This led to us making low quality stuff to hit the numbers and almost broke the company since we were faced with a ridiculous situation of optimising for a certain number of minutes. 
- Target CPM of the content
- Google had presold advertising inventory and worked backwards when calculating the value of the grants. 
- These calculations later turned out to be wildly wrong
- This skewed all of the funding they did in this project.
- Subscribers
- This led to all sorts of unintended approaches from teams
- Quality went out of the window (the entire purpose of the funding)
- The grant was spent on user acquisition and not content (again devaluing the whole initiative).


In the end Google wrote off most of the funding. 

The companies that succeeded ([including ours](https://copa90.media)) were those that did so by operating outside of the bounds of the grant structure, ignoring the metrics we were set and evolving as we went. 

I don't know why this focus on metrics is relevant - or needed, even [@raymondz](/straightedge/account/str186wygrqrgykzcr5s0alajur0p2ddc7qe8fxdkz) appears open to this discussion evolving past made up numbers.
I'm not in support of such a subjective rubric for success. I believe metrics are an effective tool here, and that quantified expectations of return are also helpful.

> This leaves me with one reservation, which is that the Agency proposal is listed to provide three ecosystem partners. If there is to be no ecosystem partner structure, other than our usual grants -- 'traditional partners,' then we will be unable to fulfill and prioritize that item. 
I think given the emergent nature of the project and the shifting challenges and capabilities of the underlying technology and the gradual process that is the community finding its voice and expressing its will via on-chain governance and proposals you should give more flexibility to the "ecosystem partner" proposition.

In the end I see Ecosystem Partner as an organised group who are pushing forwards with explicit intention to **deliver something** and this is validated via the proposal process and a series of on-chain funded projects that are successfully delivered in a phased manner.

Given our experience with the Agency and indeed in discussions with new teams and projects I think there is a relatively clear stepped process that could work as a more "structured" ecoystem proposal that removes the need for metrics, but perhaps pushes towards [@Thom Ivy](/edgeware/account/jKauGVPCQkteGTDKuuNwhYhMBrj5QuytgybEC4A5cS4Bki5) and [@raymondz](/edgeware-testnet/account/5G8jA2TLTQqnofx2jCE1MAtaZNqnJf1ujv7LdZBv2LGznJE2) ambitions for deeper economic alignment.

This builds on the thinking I first outlined in my previous post: [Edgeware Grant Programme Structure](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/1110-edgeware-grant-programme-structure-discussion) and can be applied to easily to anyone, no matter their project.

It is vital for those who wish to receive funds spend time in and around the community, because in the end we are all building on the same foundations and share the same resources and this knowledge sharing is also fundamental to us scaling our overall connectedness and culture.

- **Phase 1 grant: R&D **
- A team arrives with an idea, concept or initiative
- They discuss the project with the community 
- They share their work to date, concepts
- The community feeds back and we refine an initial proposal. 
- This leads to a community AMA which involves the wider community and gives a chance for unexpected questions or prompts to bubble up.


I see no reason why ANY team - no matter their experience or capabilities would not engage in this initial scoping process in public. If they are experienced then this process is likely to be quicker and reach resolution faster - so much the better.

- **Phase 2 grant: MVP funding**
- We fund the team to deliver an MVP of their project.
- We limit the complexity and seek to learn as much as possible.
- We use our core community as beta testers since they are the most engaged and interested.


- **Phase 3 grant: Scaled retainer**
- Inspired by the evolution of the Edgeware Agency
- We assume that with an MVP and some early users we now need to give the team time and space to continue their experimentation and to flex the project in many directions as things shift in their experience and expectations. 
- They receive ongoing stream funding that provides a solid base for them to be comfortable that they can operate on a longer time horizon but also to ensure that the Edgeware community is providing them with reassurances around their ability to earn a meaningful stake in the network over time.
- As noted this is not just a retainer, but a **scaled retainer**, meaning as projects find some sort of momentum building, they can scale up their funding request, or equally the reverse can be true, some may find the need to scale down their funding as a project reaches maturity or the team decide to work on something new.


- **Phase 4 grant: Maintenance**
- Once a project reaches maturity it may well downsize its team as noted above, equally the team may disperse and/or be interested on working on other things. If this is the case the cycle just begins again as they return to Phase 1. 
- However the project may well have become important to Edgeware and associated projects inside and outside of the ecosystem and so will need to be maintained on an ongoing basis.
- This maintenance resource can be centrally managed over time by the Agency, gradually expanding its staffing and capabiltiies and ensuring long term community alignment and tending to the shared utilities, resources and initiatives funded by the treasury.  
- This is akin to a team handing over the project to the community as a public good, keeping everyone and everything in long term alignment. 
- In this example we would offer maintenance grants, in the same spirit as [the Polkascan team](https://github.com/polkascan/social-contract/blob/master/polkadot/social-contract-002.md). 


> Polkascan Foundation has budgeted the maintenance of these libraries and provisioning of adequate community support at an estimated sum of EUR 90,000.00 on an annual basis. This should give a sustainable budget that gets Polkascan 0.80 FTU for a Senior Python Developer with substantial knowledge of Substrate.

I feel like this approach can provide the structure the Ecoystem Partners approach requires and enables the long term financial and governance alignment. 

It also removes the onerous and potential misalignment of metrics based funding which may or may not be intentionally gamed, but always has the effect of changing the intention of teams over the long term in subtle or more explicit, but always unexpected ways. 

We will be putting this structure forward as a test case in the upcoming New Futures proposal which we are very close to concluding and will help us test assumptions and experiment with the process in the real world.

I would also encourage others to think of projects that either exist or that could leverage this approach.

This leaves me with one reservation, which is that the Agency proposal is listed to provide three ecosystem partners. If there is to be no ecosystem partner structure, other than our usual grants -- 'traditional partners,' then we will be unable to fulfill and prioritize that item.

Instead, I will pivot instead to recruiting one core team, which I believe is essential to Edgeware's long term success, and treat that process as a one-off to be negotiated with the community ad-hoc. 

We will of course continue the traditional grant structure, ongoing business development and launch support.

To respond to Ramsey's Qs:

1. Is Edgeware Agency the best current example of what would be a suitable candidate? At what stage would Edgeware Agency get 4% of supply? This would give a large portion of influence over governance to a small group of people. While perhaps necessary in the short term, doesn't make sense to incentivise for it over long term?


**Yes and no. Our proposal shows a list of concrete deliverables and performance metrics, a mix.  We're also not the kind of highly-performant talent technically that we are lacking, we are a community-based management group. The Agency was formed becasue the ad-hoc agreements between the chain and multiple contractors left their activities with poor structure. The EP structure is intended to attract top tier, external talent and highly structured teams to the ecosystem.**

** I believe that the best teams we can attract may not need the funds per se to complete development, but bring massive awareness, partners, and they are looking for alignment on issues of platform and governance risk.**

**To my knowledge, only core teams have attained this kind of agreement, via a kind of tacit consent of distribution. That is a major inspiration for this project: that we do not have a core team. **

1. Do you see Edgeware take a stake in these partners?

**Token swaps are a negotiable, yes. Airdrops are a negotiable. Some projects may not have tokens themselves. **

1. Could these projects be given a standard model of governance?

**I think this is unwise, use cases demand different structures.**

1. Why would Defi project be a suitable candidate as a custodian? Is it fundamentally important? How do you define Defi? I personally think Defi is risky long term if we are considering unregulated usurious casino projects. I would back Defi projects that are Shariah compliant, which follow the simple principal of finance secured against underlying assets, where risk is shared between parties for real economic gain, rather than profiteering from transactional over-leveraged instruments leading to toxicity and collapse of systemd. There should be a compliance **standard** for Defi.


**What is a 'custodian?' Community will be empowered to approve projects they deem a good value or cultural fit. Launching on EDG is permissionless,  but we can apply per-project-basis critique on norms and technicals. I'm not interested in a hard and fast rule, in favor of a more pragmatic approach.**

Treasury management and technical committees

- Like a country, the one whole treasury is split by category into smaller treasuries.

- If the treasury requires expertise, then a committee can be created that decide on proposals that fall into that treasury.

- decide on treasury proposals

- either depending on context.

If the issue is metrics, then I think this has been a pretty good discussion, and we can move forward with some actual EP proposals to conduct the deliberation there.

To Rich's comments, as a chain we're asking for way too much. From TG chat:

> I would have a hard time advocating for [a serious project] to deploy on Edgeware unless there were a clear path to longer term alignment. As is, Edgeware is governed by mainly nontechnical users, including one who is anonymous and holds five council seats. This isn’t an appropriate foundation for a project that aims to acquire a large user base of ordinary people who will not tolerate technical issues or platform irregularities. If they secured a small EDG grant, and then became very successful, I’d have to advocate for them becoming a parachain or moving to another platform with less governance risk. If they secured a large EDG grant, then they could use their reach to hire a core dev to support EDG resolve those issues.

Holders have a huge voice in EDG governance right now, while builders do not:

> We distributed EDG to ETH holders without cost, which means we should feel free to conduct more economic experiments where a chain like Moonbeam would not be able to. Basically, we gave holders a voice but not builders - That led to the set of projects that we have now. The EP grant should give builders a voice.

We only need a few good ecosystem partners for Edgeware to work:

> Most successful chains pick a couple of things to do, and do them well. Terra built Mirror and Anchor, and that provided the foundation for all of their growth after. Solana ran a very strong BD game. It is totally unclear to me right now what that is for Edgeware. Funding is not that, the outcome and results of the funding is.

I totally agree with Rich on that alignment and commitment is something that teams show over long term. If a given team does not think of Edgeware as a target for its deployment, incentivizing it with funds is the worst thing to do, since nothing would prevent them to optimizing the metrics, and launch competing projects outside, or under some other names.

Since there is mention of "media networks" I can play it through as a prospective beneficiary of this structure.

no of chains launched?

body:
As a co-author on the proposal, I'd like to stress the importance of Edgeware having a solid structure for partnering with committed teams.

This proposal basically asks, **should Edgeware be open to granting several percent of the network (equivalent of ~$1m right now) to teams who are committed partners, if they achieve metrics on the level of "successfully building an app on the network"**. Each EDG grant would potentially be subject to a long vesting schedule after being awarded, and the exact award would also require approval from either the community or the Agency.

Each ecosystem partner proposal would also be subject to the same review process as any other proposal, so there would be a lot of oversight over the exact metrics.

I think the idea of an active-governed smart contract run by the public sector is still appealing to many teams. With this in place, Thom and the Agency would be able to go out to a far broader set of teams and propose for them to come to Edgeware.
